L29: Uniswap (UNI) futures are live on CME Group for the Oct. 19 trade date, adding a regulated derivatives product tied to a decentralized finance token to the exchange’s cryptocurrency lineup.
L30: 
L31: Standard futures cover 10,000 UNI per contract, while Micro futures cover 1,000 UNI. The Micro contract represents one-tenth as many tokens as the standard version, a difference of 9,000 UNI per contract. The two sizes give participants a choice of contract amounts while keeping both products tied to the same asset.
L32: UNI is the governance token of the Uniswap Protocol, a decentralized exchange. The futures listing widens institutional access to derivatives tied to decentralized finance through a regulated U.S. market. The contracts provide exposure to UNI, rather than to the Uniswap Protocol as a whole.
L33: 
L34: CME Group also offers futures tied to Chainlink, placing the UNI contracts within an existing range of crypto-linked futures. The trade date listed for the Uniswap products is Oct. 19, 2026.

L98: # Uniswap Protocol Fees
L99: 
L100: Understand how protocol fees flow from Uniswap products into TokenJar and through releaser contracts.
L101: 
L102: Fees from protocol versions (v2, v3, v4, UniswapX, Unichain) flow into a single onchain collector on each network. From there, specialized contracts handle how those assets are released or transformed (for example, burning UNI).
L103: ## cite17†Flow of Assets L104: 
L105:   1. Fee Sources Each protocol component that generates fees (v2, v3, v4, UniswapX, Unichain, and others) routes those fees through an associated Fee Adapter contract. Adapters define how and when fees are collected and send them to the TokenJar on the same chain.
L106: 
L107:   2. TokenJar Each chain has one immutable contract called the TokenJar. All fee sources send tokens here. It’s the unified collection point for raw tokens.
L108:   3. Releasers Releasers define how tokens in the TokenJar are accessed. The simplest version burns UNI in exchange for the collected tokens. Other Releasers could handle cross-chain conversions or alternative value flows.
L109: 
L110:   4. Governance Control Governance can update which Releaser a TokenJar uses or adjust configuration on Fee Adapters, but the core contracts themselves are immutable.
L111: ## cite18†Components L112: 
L113: ### cite19†TokenJar L114: 
L115: Immutable contract that receives all tokens from fee sources on a given chain. Only the active Releaser can withdraw from it.
L116: 
L117: See the cite20†TokenJar contract source†github.com for more.
L118: 
L119: ### cite21†Fee adapters L120: 
L121: Adapters that connect specific protocol versions or products to the TokenJar. They define how and when fees are collected.
L122: 
L123: See the cite22†Fee Adapter contract sources†github.com for more.
L124: ### cite23†Releasers L125: 
L126: Contracts that convert collected fees into protocol value according to defined logic. Examples include the Firepit Releaser, which burns UNI in return for assets.
L127: 
L128: See the cite24†Releaser contract sources†github.com for more.
L129: ## cite25†Real-World Example L130: 
L131:   * Assume 100 UNI is the `threshold` amount for the Firepit Releaser.
L132:   * When the top N assets in the TokenJar are worth slightly more than 100 UNI, anyone is incentivized to use the `Firepit.release()` contract to:
L133:     1. Burn 100 UNI
L134:     2. Withdraw the top N assets, valued at slightly more than 100 UNI
L135: 
L136: ## cite26†Firepit Mechanics L137: ### cite27†Threshold L138: 
L139: `Firepit.threshold()` is the minimum UNI amount required to call `release()`. Governance can update this threshold through the configured governance flow.
L140: 
L141: ### cite28†Release L142: 
L143: `Firepit.release()` is user-triggered. The caller submits the transaction with their signer and burns the required UNI amount to withdraw configured assets from the releaser flow.
